trial.title: At-Home Transcutaneous Tibial Nerve Stimulation for Overactive Bladder in Rural Women

endpoints.measure: Overactive Bladder questionnaire short form (OAB-q SF) Health-related Quality of life
endpoints.time_frame: Evaluated upon enrollment and following 12 weeks of intervention
endpoints.description: A 13-item survey assessing health-related quality of life. Assessed on a scale from 1 to 100 with a higher score representing a better quality of life.

endpoints.measure: Overactive Bladder questionnaire short form (OAB-q SF) symptom bother
endpoints.time_frame: Evaluated upon enrollment and following 12 weeks of intervention
endpoints.description: A 13-item survey assessing symptom bother related to overactive bladder. Assessed on a scale from 1 to 100 with a higher score representing more bother, which is a worse outcome.

endpoints.time_frame: 3-day voiding diary completed upon enrollment and following 12 weeks of intervention
endpoints.description: Mean 24-hour voiding frequency based on a 3-day voiding diary

outcome.rationale: Mixed evidence from prior TTNS trials: Welk 2020 sham-controlled trial showed no significant benefit for TTNS alone, while Barbosa 2026 showed benefit when combined with behavioral therapy. Single-arm design without sham control limits ability to detect true efficacy vs placebo. Small sample size (n=38) and rural population adherence concerns add uncertainty. Primary endpoints are patient-reported outcomes susceptible to placebo effects. Predicted modest improvements across endpoints but confidence is low due to methodological limitations and heterogeneous prior evidence.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT07178314 is a single-arm study evaluating at-home transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (TTNS) for overactive bladder (OAB) in rural women. The study uses a 12-week intervention period with three 30-minute sessions per week.

Evidence from Welk et al. 2020 (PMC7337720) shows a randomized sham-controlled trial of TTNS for OAB found no significant difference between active TTNS and sham for PPBC responder rates (15% vs 13%, p=0.77) or voiding diary parameters. This suggests limited efficacy of TTNS alone.

Evidence from Barbosa et al. 2026 (PLOS ONE) shows TTNS combined with behavioral therapy improved urgency and nocturia vs behavioral therapy alone in older women, suggesting TTNS has adjunctive efficacy when combined with other interventions.
The current trial is single-arm without sham control, which introduces placebo response bias. OAB trials typically show 20-40% placebo response rates for patient-reported outcomes.

OAB-q SF (Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Short Form) is a validated PRO measure with scores 0-100. Higher scores indicate better HRQoL for primary-0 and more bother (worse) for primary-1. MCID for OAB-q SF is approximately 10-15 points based on prior OAB literature.
Voiding frequency in OAB is typically 8+ voids/day at baseline. Clinically meaningful reduction is 1-2 voids/day or 15-25% reduction.

Based on mixed evidence: Welk 2020 showed no significant benefit vs sham for TTNS alone; Barbosa 2026 showed benefit when combined with behavioral therapy. This trial uses TTNS alone without behavioral therapy as a structured component.

Predictions assume modest improvement due to: (1) placebo/expectancy effects in single-arm design, (2) natural variability in OAB symptoms, (3) potential true neuromodulatory effect, but (4) evidence from sham-controlled trials suggests limited specific efficacy.
Primary uncertainties: lack of sham control, small sample size (n=38), rural population adherence to at-home protocol, and heterogeneity in prior TTNS trial results.
Safety: TTNS is generally well-tolerated with minimal adverse events reported in prior trials.
